title: Add vincent workflow init
body:
## Summary

Adds `vincent workflow init <name> [--from <example>] [--project N] [--json]`:
writes a valid workflow YAML file into the right registry directory, prints the
path, and refuses to damage anything already there.

Nothing in the binary helped you write your first workflow. The CLI's workflow
surface was `ls` and `validate`, neither of which creates anything, and the TUI
deliberately does not either (spec §15 view 5 — untouched here). So anything past
a one-step ad-hoc run meant reading the schema reference, finding `examples/`,
copying one, working out which of the two scope directories it belongs in, and
validating in hope. The docs carry all of that; the tool never mentioned it, and
a user with the binary on their `$PATH` and no checkout in front of them had no
command that produced a valid file in the right directory.

**Daemon split, mirroring the one already in the package.** The default (global)
scope resolves `{config_dir}/workflows/` from `internal/config` with no daemon at
all. `--project N` contacts one purely to resolve the id to a repository root,
and exits **2** without writing when none answers. `validate` is daemon-free by
design; `ls` needs a daemon because only it knows which projects exist (PR U
decision). `init` is daemon-free in its default shape and daemon-bound only in
the branch that genuinely needs a project lookup.

**`--from` hands over the shipped examples, comments included.** A new root
`examples` package embeds `examples/*.yaml` — `go:embed` reads only its own
package tree, the same constraint that put `skills/embed.go` where it is, so the
embed reads the real published files rather than a copy that can drift
(`.goreleaser.yaml` already globs the same files, so the release archive is
unaffected). Both the accepted values and the unknown-value error's list come
from that filesystem at run time, so a sixth example is offered the day it lands.
Only the top-level `name:` line is rewritten, as text: a round trip through
`goccy/go-yaml` would drop exactly the comments that make an example worth
handing over. Column zero is the whole rule, and it is exact — in block context a
`- name:` under `fields:`, a `name:` inside a step and a `name:` inside a
`prompt:` block scalar are all indented past the key that opens them.

*One accepted cost, recorded in the task document so it is not later filed as a
bug:* the written file's header comment still reads `# feature-pr — implement a
change…` while its `name:` reads `<name>`. Rewriting that prose too would have
`init` editing text it does not own, under a rule that breaks the moment an
example's header changes shape.

**With no `--from`, a commented one-agent-step skeleton.** It lives in
`internal/workflow` beside `AdhocSource` and `CreateWorkflowSource` so the
package that owns `Parse` can hold it to the bar a shipped example is held to —
zero errors *and* zero warnings. Its comments name what a first author otherwise
misses: `command` and `manual`, `check` as a *field* on agent and command steps
rather than a fourth type, `max_retries`, `timeout`, and a pointer to
`docs/reference/workflow-schema.md`.

**Collisions: refuse on the file, warn on the shadow.** The target path is opened
with `O_CREATE|O_EXCL`, so "never clobber" is a syscall guarantee rather than a
stat-then-write race. A *name* another file in the same scope already declares is
refused too — that is the collision the file name hides. The registry keys on
`name:` and the first file by sorted path wins, so a sibling sorting *before* the
new file would leave it invalid, and one sorting *after* would be invalidated by
it; both directions are damage, so both are refused, naming the file that holds
the name. A sibling that does not parse has no knowable name and cannot block
anything — it is already visible as an invalid entry in `workflow ls`. Shadowing
a *lower* scope is §5.2 working as designed and only warns, and the help text
says plainly which direction the warning cannot see: a global workflow may be
shadowed later by a project file in any repository, which no daemon-free command
can know.

**`<name>` is held to `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]*$`**, not the looser §8.2 rule for a
`name:` field, because it is also a file name — the dual role behind task 024
decision 10 — and the same name must be legal by both routes into the registry.

**It ships alongside `create-workflow`, not instead of it.** The issue's premise
that `adhoc` is the only built-in is stale: task 024 landed `create-workflow` on
2026-08-23. The gap is nonetheless real and the two do not overlap in practice —
`create-workflow` needs a daemon, a registered project, an authenticated agent
CLI and a task run that costs tokens and holds a concurrency slot while it may
park in `awaiting_input`; `init` is offline, free, instant and deterministic.
Task 024 rejected nothing about a CLI affordance, so nothing binding is reopened,
but the two are now positioned against each other in the docs and in each
command's help text rather than left to compete.

## Related

Closes #96.
Closes 031.1–031.5 (`docs/tasks/031-workflow-init.md`).

Consumes, without changing, §5.2's shadowing and first-file-wins rules and task
024 decision 10 (the name/file-name dual role). Does **not** revisit the spec §15
view 5 / §19 M3 decision that the TUI has no create path — this is a CLI
affordance only.

## Checklist

- [x] PR title is plain language (no Conventional Commit prefix)
- [x] Commits follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/)
- [x] Tests added/updated for behavior changes
- [ ] User-visible changes noted under `## [Unreleased]` in `CHANGELOG.md` —
      **deliberately not done.** `RELEASING.md` (step 3) records that this file
      carries no `Unreleased` section on purpose: Release Please inserts each new
      version directly beneath the preamble, so an `Unreleased` heading is pushed
      *below* the release it describes and the released entry keeps its
      mechanical commit list. That is the exact damage `fd7f7f0` was written to
      clean up. The `feat(cli):` commit subject is what Release Please picks up;
      the prose belongs in the release PR and in `site-changelog.md` at release
      time.
- [x] Affected page under `docs/` updated (config, CLI, API, TUI keys, block reasons)

**Spec.** `docs/spec.md` §12.1's CLI table said `vincent workflow ls / validate
[file]`, which this makes untrue. Amended in place with a dated note
(*Amended 2026-08-26 (task 031)*) stating the command and the daemon-free /
daemon-bound split. §5.2 needs **no** amendment: `init` changes no registry
semantics, it only consumes rules already written there.

**Docs.** `docs/reference/cli.md` gains `### vincent workflow init` (flags, the
name rule, both collision behaviours, exit codes, and the `init` vs
`create-workflow` positioning), and its exit-code table row for `1` is corrected
— it claimed "the daemon answered and rejected the request", which was never true
of `workflow validate` and is not true of `init` either. `README.md`,
`docs/getting-started/quickstart.md` and `docs/guides/workflows.md` now lead with
`vincent workflow init` instead of the platform-split `cp examples/...` /
`copy examples\...` blocks, and say when to reach for `create-workflow` instead.

A documentation audit over the whole tree then found four more places that
`init` had made untrue, fixed in a separate `docs:` commit. Three were the same
claim from different angles — that `workflow validate` is the *only* subcommand
that runs without a daemon: `docs/guides/scripting.md` counted "two commands
work with no daemon" and added "everything else exits 2"; `docs/reference/cli.md`
called validate "the one command that needs no daemon" in its own section, one
screen below the new `init` section that contradicts it; and `README.md` still
described exit `1` as "the daemon answered and rejected the request", the
sentence `docs/reference/cli.md`'s exit-code table had already been corrected
for. The fourth is `docs/features.md`, whose closing call to action sent a
reader off to copy an example file by hand; it now names `init` and keeps the
examples as its `--from` values.

The rest of the derivations were checked and needed nothing: no route, binding,
config key, `Reason*` constant, step type, schema field or adapter capability
moved, so `docs/reference/api.md`, `docs/guides/tui.md`,
`docs/reference/configuration.md`, `docs/reference/workflow-schema.md`,
`docs/reference/task-lifecycle.md` and `docs/guides/agents.md` are untouched by
design. `skills/vincent-workflows/SKILL.md` is runtime text spliced into the
`create-workflow` prompt and is **not** part of this PR: the schema it teaches
did not change, and its instruction to write the file to
`.vincent/workflows/<name>.yaml` is still exactly right. No TUI panel changed,
so no capture under `docs/assets/` is stale. This repository's own
`.vincent/workflows/*.yaml` are unaffected for the same reason the schema
reference is.

## Testing

`go run mage.go test` — 30 packages, all green. `go run mage.go lint` clean, and
clean again under `GOOS=windows`, `GOOS=darwin` and `GOOS=linux` per CLAUDE.md's
cross-lint recipe. Every path is built with `filepath`; no new platform-specific
code was needed.

New coverage, in the package that owns each fact:

*`internal/workflow`* — the skeleton parses with zero errors and zero warnings
under the same curated catalogs `TestShippedExamplesValidate` uses (the two now
share one options helper), and still does after the rename. Every embedded
example parses clean *after* the rewrite, table-driven over `examples.Names()`,
so a new example cannot land as a broken `--from` value. The rewrite is held to
the top-level key alone against a fixture carrying a header comment repeating the
old name, a `- name:` under `fields:`, a `name:` nested in a step and a `name:`
inside a `prompt:` block scalar — asserted both as a whole-string comparison and
per surviving line — plus CRLF preservation, and comment-character and line
counts over every real example.

*`internal/cli`* — each refusal exits non-zero **and leaves the tree
byte-identical** (snapshot compare): an existing target path, a re-run of the
same command, a sibling declaring the name in both sort orders (`aaa.yaml` and
`zzz.yml`), six rejected `<name>` values, and an unknown `--from` whose error is
checked to list every valid one. `--project` with no daemon exits 2 and writes
nothing; against a stub daemon it resolves the root, writes into
`.vincent/workflows/`, and warns without blocking when the name is held globally
or by a built-in. An unknown project id is exit 1, not 2, and creates no
directory.

*e2e, through the real binary* — the cold start (`init` with no daemon writes
into `VINCENT_CONFIG_DIR/workflows`, records no `daemon.json`, and the written
file then passes `vincent workflow validate`), and live reload (with a daemon up,
`init` global and `init --project 1 --from fix-and-test` both appear in
`vincent workflow ls --project 1` with no restart, in the right scope and not as
invalid entries).

No new gate script: this is a CLI command with deterministic output and no daemon
choreography worth driving over curl, and the e2e tests cover it at the right
level.

title: Restore the MIT license
body:
## Summary

- restore the MIT License across the repository, documentation, release archives, and package-manager metadata
- remove the separate commercial license and update release validation accordingly
- preserve historical licensing records while marking the old packaging decision superseded
- track the CodeGraph `.gitignore` while keeping its machine-local database and runtime files excluded

## Validation

- `go run mage.go test`
- `go run ./cmd/vincent workflow validate .vincent/workflows/release.yaml` (0 warnings)
- YAML parsing for `.goreleaser.yaml` and `.github/workflows/release.yml`
- license consistency audit and `git diff --check`

title: Add a per-task cost cap enforced at attempt boundaries
body:
## Summary

Cost was measured and never acted on. `step_runs.cost_usd` is written from the
adapter's terminal `result` line, rolled up across every attempt by
`store.TaskRollups`, and rendered on the board and detail views — and nothing in
the engine, the scheduler or the store ever read it to decide anything.

That left a gap between the two guards that do exist. `agent_timeout` bounds one
attempt's wall clock; `transcript_max_bytes` bounds its bytes on disk. An agent
that loops *productively* — quick turns, modest output, no hang — trips neither,
and can spend its full `agent_timeout` per attempt across the whole retry budget
with nothing but a human noticing to stop it.

This adds one configured ceiling on one task's rolled-up spend, checked by the
engine at every attempt boundary, that blocks the task with a new `cost_limit`
reason.

**Configuration.** New top-level key `max_task_cost_usd`, beside
`transcript_max_bytes` rather than under `defaults:` (timeouts a step may
override — PR V decision). Zero is the default and means no cap, so nothing
changes for anyone who does not ask; a negative value fails the load. A plain
`float64` rather than a `Duration`/`ByteSize`-style string, because USD is
already the unit and it is in the key name. Hot reload needed no work: the
engine reads `r.deps.Config()` per check, the way the transcript cap is read per
attempt.

**Enforcement.** `ReasonCostLimit = "cost_limit"`, and the check lives in
`runStepWithRetries` immediately after the attempt's row is finished — not in
`runSteps`, which walks top-level positions only. A `loop` is one such position
and a `parallel` group's sub-steps are reduced by `collectGroup`, so a check
there would let a fifty-iteration loop, or a step's whole `max_retries` budget,
run before the cap was consulted once. The verdict rides out on
`stepOutcome.costExceeded`, which inherits `backoffUntil`'s standing rule
verbatim — every branch that turns an outcome into something else tests it
first: `collectGroup`'s new first tier, the `allow_failure` arm in `group.go`,
and `runBodyStep`'s early return in `loop.go`, which also covers the branch that
*discards* a successful body step's outcome and is what makes the cap fire
mid-loop rather than after it.

**It is a block, not a step failure.** The finished `step_run` keeps its own
state and its own reason, no retry is consumed, and a retry that was already due
does not run — retrying spends more money to arrive at the same wall, which
pre-empts task 028's `retry_backoff` re-queue with it. `r.fail(…)` is
`taskstate.Fail`: no new FSM edge, no `taskstate` change, no migration, no
`tasks` column. The step cursor deliberately does not advance, so a retry
resumes the step the task is blocked at (and a group or loop resumes from its
rows); because the check runs only *after* an attempt finishes, that retry makes
exactly one attempt of progress before blocking again. `resume` is not the
escape hatch — it is valid only from `paused`.

**Scope and gaps, stated rather than papered over.** The cap counts **one
task**: a `fan_out` lane is an ordinary task row, so a twenty-lane tree may
spend twenty times it. It is inert on codex and cursor, guarded by
`store.TaskRollup.HasCost` as well as by `> cap`, so "unreported" and "genuinely
free" stay different facts and nothing is estimated from token counts. And the
attempt that crosses the line runs to completion: cost arrives on the terminal
result line and nowhere else, so there is no mid-run signal to poll.

**Surfaces.** `max_task_cost_usd` on `GET /v1/config` and `apiclient.Config`
(the TUI reads no configuration from disk, §15), and the daemon view's config
block, where zero renders `off` and never `$0.00`.

## Related

Closes #97

Closes 031.1, 031.2, 031.3, 031.4 — `docs/tasks/031-task-cost-cap.md` records
the six decisions and the alternative each beat, including the two that revise
the issue as filed: the key is `max_task_cost_usd` and per-task rather than the
proposed global `max_cost_usd` (a daemon-global promise the code does not keep
is worse than an honest per-task one), and the issue's open question about
`resume` rests on a wrong premise — `resume` is valid only from `paused`, so the
escape hatch is `retry`, which advances by one attempt and re-blocks.

Reaffirms, does not revisit: PR V's "`defaults:` is timeouts" (the key sits at
the top level), task 014 decision 1 ("a lane is an ordinary task" — which is
what makes the cap per-task rather than per-tree), task 028's precedence rule
for `backoffUntil` (extended, not changed), and PR I's "cost is the sum of every
attempt, not the surviving one" (now load-bearing rather than reporting).

## Checklist

- [x] PR title is plain language (no Conventional Commit prefix)
- [x] Commits follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/)
- [x] Tests added/updated for behavior changes
- [ ] User-visible changes noted under `## [Unreleased]` in `CHANGELOG.md` —
      **not done, deliberately.** `CHANGELOG.md` carries no `Unreleased` section
      and must not gain one: Release Please inserts each new version directly
      beneath the preamble, so an `Unreleased` block is pushed *below* the
      release it describes. `RELEASING.md` step 3 pins the changelog (both of
      them) to the Release Please pull request, which is where this entry
      belongs. The `feat(taskrun):` commit is what puts it there.
- [x] Affected page under `docs/` updated (config, CLI, API, TUI keys, block reasons)

### Tests

Engine tests against `cmd/fakeagent`, whose claude dialect already reports
`total_cost_usd: 0.0123`, so no new scenario was needed
(`internal/taskrun/costlimit_test.go`):

- a cap below that blocks `cost_limit` after the first attempt, the second step
  never runs, and the `step_run` row is `succeeded` with an empty failure reason
  — the whole "block, not fail" claim;
- unset (`0`), generous, and exactly-equal caps all run to `done`;
- no retry consumed: `CountStepAttempts` at the blocked position shows one
  attempt and no failure, and a `retry` takes it to exactly two before
  re-blocking `cost_limit`;
- the cap beats a step failure with budget left — `max_retries: 2` plus
  `retry_backoff: 30s` against the `nonzero-exit` scenario (which reports cost
  *and* exits 3): one row, `failed`/`nonzero_exit`, no `queued_reason`, no
  `step.retrying` event;
- it fires **inside** a loop: `count: 3` over an agent body blocks on iteration
  1 with one row, which is the test that distinguishes the chosen enforcement
  point from the rejected one;
- inert on codex and cursor: both run to `done` under a `0.000001` cap and
  `HasCost` stays false;
- the documented remedy end to end: raise the cap on a running daemon, retry,
  finish.

Plus config load/reject/default cases naming the key, a `GET /v1/config` test
for the served value, and a daemon-view test that an unset cap renders `off` and
never `$0.00`.

`go run mage.go test` and `go run mage.go lint` are green, the latter
cross-checked for `GOOS=windows`, `darwin` and `linux`; `go test -race
./internal/taskrun` is clean (the engine harness's config is now behind a
`sync.RWMutex` so a test can stage a hot reload). Nothing here is
platform-specific and no new gate script was added: this is engine behaviour
with a config input, which `internal/taskrun` proves directly, and there is no
human judgement in it of the kind M3 and task 017 have.

### Spec

Amended in place and dated 2026-08-26, in this same PR: **§12.3** for the key,
its per-task scope and the fan-out multiplication; **§17** for the shift from
measured to enforced (the "aggregate cost across attempts" sentence is now
load-bearing); **§18** for a new edge-case row covering the reason, the
one-attempt overshoot, the retry semantics and the inert-on-codex/cursor
behaviour.

Pages updated: `docs/reference/configuration.md` (the key),
`docs/reference/task-lifecycle.md` and `docs/guides/troubleshooting.md` (the new
block reason and the "raise it and retry" remedy, including that retrying
without raising it costs one more attempt each time), plus
`docs/guides/agents.md`, `docs/guides/workflows.md` and `docs/faq.md`, whose
existing cost paragraphs were true but incomplete once the figure became a
limit.

A later documentation-only commit adds three things the first pass was short
of: `docs/features.md`, which enumerates every other bound a run has —
timeouts, retry counts, usage-limit waits, `retry_backoff` — and had nothing on
spend; and, in `docs/reference/configuration.md` and
`docs/guides/troubleshooting.md`, **what the figure actually counts**.
`store.TaskRollups` is `SUM(cost_usd)` over every `step_runs` row of the task,
so a repair run and a follow-up round count toward the cap and the total never
resets. The consequence is not guessable from the pages as written: a finished
task already over the cap blocks `cost_limit` on the first attempt of its next
follow-up, where `skip` returns it to `done`.

### Found in this pass, not fixed here

Both are for the reviewer to decide on; neither is a documentation change.

- **The merge resolver drops the cost verdict.** `internal/taskrun/join.go:241`
  runs the agent merge resolver through `runStepWithRetries` and then tests only
  `attempt.state`: on success it returns a fresh `stepOutcome{}`, on failure the
  prebuilt `blocked` one, so `costExceeded` is discarded on both paths. That is
  the same branch class decision 2 names — "every branch that turns an outcome
  into something else must test it first" — and it is the one that was not
  covered. The effect: a resolver attempt that takes the task past the cap does
  not stop it there, and because the resolver runs per conflicted lane, a join
  can run several such attempts before the next ordinary boundary blocks the
  task. It does not make the cap unenforced, but it does make "you overshoot by
  at most one attempt" untrue for this path, which is a claim §18, the config
  reference and the troubleshooting page all make. A fix is a few lines in
  `resolveConflict` plus a `join`-shaped test; the documented promise is the
  thing to keep.

- **Task ID 031 is already taken on `origin/master`.** This branch forked at
  `8511551` and claimed `031`; master has since merged
  `docs/tasks/031-native-process-identity.md` and
  `docs/tasks/032-macos-notarization.md`. Rebasing conflicts only in
  `docs/tasks/README.md` — the two documents themselves merge cleanly side by
  side — so the duplicate can survive a careless resolution. This wants
  renumbering to **033** on the rebase: the file, its index row, the `§12.3`,
  `§17` and `§18` amendments in `docs/spec.md`, and the `task 031` citations in
  `internal/config/config.go`, `internal/api/server.go`,
  `internal/apiclient/daemon.go`, `internal/tui/daemonrender.go`,
  `internal/taskrun/engine.go`, `internal/taskrun/group.go`,
  `internal/taskrun/loop.go` and `internal/taskrun/repair.go`. It was left alone
  here deliberately: renumbering the documents without the code comments would
  point every citation at a real but unrelated task.

No screenshot is stale. `configLines` gained a "max task cost" line in the
daemon view, and there is no `docs/assets/tui-daemon.png` — the daemon view is
described in prose in `docs/guides/tui.md` ("the config in effect"), which does
not enumerate the lines.

title: GitHub integration: select a GitHub issue when creating a task
body:
### Problem

Most work in a GitHub-hosted repo starts life as a GitHub issue, but vincent knows nothing about GitHub. Creating a task for an existing issue means opening the issue in a browser, copying the title into the new-task form, copying the body into the description, and then re-typing anything the workflow needs as a declared field. The issue number and URL survive only if the human remembers to paste them, and the agent that eventually runs the workflow never sees the issue's labels, author or link at all — a workflow prompt cannot say "fix the bug described below" because there is nothing in the §8.4 template context to interpolate.

Today there is no GitHub concept anywhere in the tree: `store.Project` has no remote or host field, `config.yaml` has no `github` key, and `workflow.RenderContext` has no issue surface.

### Proposed solution

When a project is GitHub-based **and** GitHub integration is enabled, let the human pick a GitHub issue while creating a task. The pick prefills the task and is carried into the workflow's template context so issue details are available to prompts and commands.

This is the first piece of a broader GitHub integration; **checking on pull requests is the intended next piece** and should not be designed out, but it is explicitly not in scope here.

**Detection and enablement.** "GitHub-based" is derived, not stored: parse the project's `origin` remote for a github.com host at the point of use. No new `Project` column and no migration. "Enabled" is a `config.yaml` toggle, so a user who does not want the daemon reading GitHub can turn it off; hot reload applies as it does for the rest of config.

**Authentication.** Prefer the `gh` CLI (`gh issue list/view --json …`) and fall back to `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GH_TOKEN` from the daemon's inherited environment when `gh` is absent or unauthenticated. vincent stores no credential of its own, which keeps spec §2's "secret management" non-goal intact and matches how the daemon already drives external CLIs. The daemon makes the call — clients never talk to GitHub, per the ownership invariant. `gitx.RemoteTimeout` is the precedent for bounding it.

**Surfaces.**

- TUI: an issue row in the new-task form, opening a picker in the same shape as the existing project/workflow/agent pickers (`internal/tui/newtaskpicker.go`). Default listing is open issues, newest first, narrowable by typed text; the row belongs in the §15 form order, before title.
- API: a `github_issue` field on `POST /v1/tasks`, plus whatever read endpoint the picker needs to list issues for a project. The TUI holds no state the daemon doesn't have, so this exists regardless of the TUI.
- CLI: `vincent task create --github-issue 123`, resolved daemon-side, with explicit flags winning over anything the issue would have prefilled; and a list command (`vincent github issues`) so issues can be browsed without opening the TUI.

**What the pick fills in.** Title from the issue title, description from the issue body, a link line carrying the issue number and URL appended to the description so a task read on its own still points back, and a best-effort mapping of issue metadata (labels, assignee, milestone) onto the workflow's declared `fields:` (§8.1.2) where the names line up. Everything lands in the form's editable rows — nothing is locked, and a human can rewrite or clear any of it before creating. Because the mapping guesses, it must be visible in the form before creation rather than applied silently at run time.

**Template context.** A new top-level `.Issue` in `workflow.RenderContext` (number, title, body, URL, state, labels, author, …), zero-valued when no issue is linked so a template shared between linked and unlinked tasks can test it — the same convention `.Loop`'s `Index: 0` already uses. Rendering must stay a pure, offline operation.

**Freshness.** The issue is fetched once at task creation and persisted on the task; every step renders from that snapshot. This is the same reasoning that makes vincent snapshot the workflow YAML at creation: a run is reproducible, no network call enters the step path, and a step render still cannot fail for an external reason. An issue edited on GitHub after task creation is deliberately not reflected.

**When GitHub is unavailable** — `gh` missing, not authenticated, no token, rate-limited, offline — the issue row is not offered and the daemon logs the concrete reason. In addition, `vincent doctor` gains a row reporting `gh` presence and authentication state, so the diagnosis lives beside the other environment checks rather than only in the daemon log.

**Acceptance criteria**

- With integration enabled and a GitHub `origin`, the TUI new-task form offers an issue picker; selecting an issue fills title, description, link line and matching declared fields, and every one of them is still editable.
- With integration disabled, or on a project whose `origin` is not GitHub, no issue row appears and no GitHub call is made.
- A task created from issue N renders `.Issue.Number`, `.Issue.Title`, `.Issue.Body`, `.Issue.URL` and `.Issue.Labels` in an agent or command step; a task created without one renders the zero value and a `{{ if .Issue.Number }}` template works on both.
- `vincent task create --github-issue N` produces the same stored task as the TUI path; explicit flags override the issue-derived values.
- `vincent github issues` lists selectable issues for a project.
- Editing the issue on GitHub after creation does not change what a later step renders.
- With `gh` absent and no token set: no issue row, a logged reason, and a `vincent doctor` row saying so — task creation without an issue is unaffected.
- Cross-platform: the `gh` invocation and the token fallback both work on Windows, macOS and Linux.

### Alternatives considered

- **Store the GitHub repo on `Project`** (`github_repo: owner/name`, auto-filled at registration, editable). Handles SSH aliases and non-`origin` GitHub remotes, and would let the projects view show the link — but it costs a migration and a new editable field for a fact that is derivable today. Worth revisiting if remote parsing proves too narrow, or when PR checking lands and needs a durable repo identity.
- **Flatten issue data into `Task.Fields`** as `github_issue_number`, `github_issue_body`, … instead of a `.Issue` struct. No new context type and it works in every existing template, but it collides with user-declared field names and flattens labels into a joined string.
- **Store a GitHub token in `config.yaml`.** Self-contained and independent of `gh`, but it makes vincent a secret store, which spec §2 declines.
- **Re-fetch the issue on every step render.** Always current, at the cost of a network call and a new failure mode inside rendering, which today cannot fail for external reasons.
- **Prefill the title only** and leave the body reachable solely through `.Issue.Body`. Keeps the description for the human's own framing, but loses the at-a-glance context on the board and in the detail view.

### Spec reference

§5.1 (Project), §5.3 (Task), §8.1.2 (declared task fields), §8.4 (template context), §13.2 (endpoints), §15 (TUI new-task form). §2 non-goal "secret management (daemon inherits the user's environment)" is what selects the `gh`/env-token approach. Decision record row 11 — "Delivery owned entirely by workflow steps; no hardcoded push/PR/merge behavior" — is not contradicted by this: reading an issue to prefill a task is input, not delivery, and no push, PR or merge behavior is added. That row does become live when PR checking arrives, so the design should keep GitHub access out of the delivery path.

title: Let a step report a custom status message, live and on failure
body:
### Problem

A step cannot say anything about itself in its own words. Today a reader has two
channels and neither answers "what is this doing" or "why did that fail":

- `failure_reason` is a **closed enum** of daemon-authored constants
  (`timeout`, `nonzero_exit`, `check_failed`, `merge_conflict`, …
  `internal/taskrun/engine.go:23`, `internal/worktree/worktree.go:22`). It says
  which *category* of thing went wrong, never which file, which test, which
  assertion. `nonzero_exit` on a 40-minute agent step is almost no information.
- `step_runs.result_summary` holds the agent's final result text or the last 200
  lines of command stdout. It is stored, exposed on the API DTO
  (`internal/api/tasks.go:234`), and read by `.Steps.<id>.Result` and the repair
  prompt — but it is **never rendered anywhere in the TUI**. The attempt line in
  `internal/tui/detailrender.go:539` shows state, duration, tokens, cost,
  `failure_reason`, `skip_reason` and the agent triple, and nothing else.

So a task that is running tells you only that it is running, and a task that is
blocked tells you only the category of its failure. Finding out more means
opening the transcript, which is the durable output copy — not a summary.

The gap is worst for the two cases in this issue's title:

1. **Live.** A `running` agent step is opaque for its whole duration. On the
   board, a row that has been running for 25 minutes looks identical whether the
   agent is scaffolding a migration or stuck retrying the same failing test.
2. **Terminal.** When a step fails, the step itself usually *knows* why in terms
   a human wants — "3 tests red in internal/store", "no upstream branch" — and
   has no way to say so. The enum flattens all of that to `check_failed`.

### Proposed solution

Let the **running step process emit its own status message**, and carry that
message through the daemon to every client.

**Producing it — a sentinel line in the step's output.** The agent or command
writes a marked line (spelling TBD, e.g. `::vincent:status:: <text>`) to its
output; the daemon recognises it in the stream it already reads and lifts it out
as the step run's current status. This was chosen over a workflow-authored
`status:` template field precisely because the interesting messages are the ones
only the step can know at run time — which test failed, which file conflicted.
A template rendered from the §8.4 context could not produce those.

Open sub-questions for the implementer:

- Where the parse hooks in. Agent steps arrive as a normalized `AgentEvent`
  stream (§9, `Output` events); command steps as raw stdout/stderr. Both funnel
  through `Runner.publishOutput` (`internal/taskrun/runner.go:302`), which is the
  natural single seam.
- Whether a matched sentinel line is **stripped from the transcript and from
  `result_summary`**, or left in place. Stripping keeps `.Steps.<id>.Result` and
  the `<previous-attempt-failure>` retry block clean; leaving it keeps the
  transcript a faithful copy of what the process printed. Prefer leaving the
  transcript untouched and stripping only from the derived summary, but this
  needs deciding, not defaulting.
- Bounds: max length, single-line only, and what happens to a step that emits
  the sentinel in a tight loop. Live output chunks are already droppable for
  slow subscribers (§13.3), but a status is *state* and needs a cap and a
  sane update rate.
- Whether an agent has to be told about the protocol in its prompt for this to
  ever fire in practice, and if so whether the daemon appends that instruction
  automatically the way it appends the retry-failure block (§8.4).

**Lifecycle — both live and terminal.** A running step may update its status any
number of times. The last value set before the attempt ends is retained on the
finished step run as its terminal message, which is what makes "why it failed"
work. So this is one field with two readings, not two features.

**Persistence and API.** A new nullable column on `step_runs` (append-only
migration, `internal/store/migrations/0014_*.sql`), a new field on the step-run
DTO in `internal/api/tasks.go` and `internal/apiclient/tasks.go`, and an SSE
signal when it changes so clients update without polling. Note the §13.3 split:
durable state events are replayable via `Last-Event-ID`, live output chunks are
dropped for slow subscribers. A status update needs to land on the **durable**
side, or a client that blinks loses the message with no way to recover it.

**Surfaces — all four are in scope:**

- TUI detail, on the attempt line beside `failure_reason`
  (`internal/tui/detailrender.go` `attemptLine`).
- TUI board, on the task row, so a running or blocked task explains itself
  without being opened. Board rows are width-constrained; this needs a
  truncation rule, not just an extra field.
- REST + SSE, so curl and scripts see it too.
- The `vincent` CLI task-inspection output.

**Step-type scope — and one thing that does not resolve.** The intent is that
*every* step type can carry a status: `agent`, `command`, `manual`, and the
structure steps (`parallel`, `fan_out`, `condition`, `loop`, `break`).
`include` is out by construction — it is spliced away at task creation (§7.9)
and never reaches the engine.

But a sentinel line requires a process to print it, and only `agent` and
`command` steps have one. `manual` waits on a human; the structure steps
evaluate templates or coordinate children. Those types record `step_run` rows
(`internal/taskrun/engine.go:742` writes the row generically from
`env.step.Type`, and `internal/taskrun/condition.go:66` does the same for
conditions) but they never run a subprocess, so the emit mechanism cannot reach
them as specified. Three ways out, and this needs a maintainer decision before
implementation:

1. Ship the sentinel for `agent` and `command` only, and leave the other types
   with an empty status — smallest change, but "all step types" is not met.
2. Add a workflow-authored `status:` template as the mechanism for the types
   with no process, so `manual` and the structure steps get their status from
   YAML while `agent`/`command` get theirs from the sentinel. Two mechanisms
   feeding one field.
3. Have the daemon synthesise a status for the process-less types from what it
   already knows (a condition's rendered guard and verdict, a loop's iteration
   and item, a group's finished/total lane count). No new authoring surface, but
   it is daemon-authored text, which is what `failure_reason` already is.

### Alternatives considered

- **A workflow-authored `status:` template field on `Step`** rendered against the
  §8.4 context. Rejected as the primary mechanism: it can only restate what the
  workflow author already knew when they wrote the YAML, so it cannot say which
  test failed or which file conflicted. Still on the table as the *secondary*
  mechanism for process-less step types (option 2 above).
- **Just render the existing `result_summary` in the TUI.** Much cheaper — no
  migration, no protocol, no new API field — and it would improve the blocked
  case immediately. Rejected as sufficient because it gives nothing while a step
  is running, and its content is whatever the process happened to print last
  rather than something the step chose to say.
- **Widening the `failure_reason` enum.** Doesn't help: the value is that the
  message is free-form and run-specific. Adding constants keeps it categorical,
  and the enum is deliberately shared vocabulary between `internal/worktree` and
  `internal/taskrun/engine.go` — a `block_reason` means the same thing wherever
  it originated, and free text would break that.
- **Telling people to read the transcript.** This is the status quo. The
  transcript is the durable output copy, not a summary; scanning it is exactly
  the work this issue asks the step to do once, for itself.

### Spec reference

New material, so it amends rather than cites:

- **§5.4 StepRun** — the field list is normative and would gain the status
  message. Note it does not currently list `result_summary` either, which is
  worth fixing in the same pass.
- **§7.2 Failure and retry** — the relationship between a free-text status and
  the `failure_reason` enum, and whether the status reaches the
  `<previous-attempt-failure>` block on retries.
- **§8.4 Template context** — only if a workflow-authored `status:` template is
  adopted for the process-less types, and if `.Steps.<id>` gains the status
  alongside `Status`/`Result`/`ExitCode`.
- **§13.3 Events** — the durable-vs-droppable split; a status update must be
  durable.
- **§15 TUI** — board row and detail attempt line.
- **§9** — whether the sentinel is parsed per-adapter or once over the
  normalized `AgentEvent` stream. Adapters differ in what they can do and those
  differences are documented, never faked, so if any adapter cannot carry the
  sentinel that has to be stated rather than emulated.

Nothing in `docs/tasks/` covers this yet; it would be task 033.

title: Answer a question longer than 256 bytes
body:
## Summary

A task parked in `awaiting_input` on a question longer than 256 bytes could not
be answered. `POST /v1/tasks/{id}/answer` refused every body with `400
validation_failed: answers key must be at most 256 bytes (got 438)`, so the task
sat holding its concurrency slot until it was cancelled or `input_timeout` (24 h
by default) expired and failed the step. The daemon parked on, persisted and
rendered a question it would then refuse every answer to.

**Root cause: one constant serving two unrelated kinds of key.**
`maxFieldKeyBytes = 256` (`internal/api/limits.go`) was applied both by
`boundTaskFields` to a `fields` key and by `boundAnswers` to an `answers` key.
Those are not the same kind of thing. A `fields` key is a caller-chosen
identifier a human or a workflow author types (§8.1.2), and 256 B is generous
for one. An `answers` key is not chosen by the caller at all: it is the agent's
verbatim question text. §7.4 makes that text the lookup key —
`taskrun.validateAnswer` matches `in.Answers[q.Text]` exactly and rejects any key
that matches no pending question — and §9.2 has the claude adapter write the
answer back to the CLI under the same text in `updatedInput.answers`. So no
layer between the agent and the answer route is permitted to shorten it, and
bounding it like an identifier made the question unanswerable rather than
truncating it.

The asymmetry in the report is the tell: `maxFieldValueBytes` is 64 KiB, so a
438-byte *answer* was fine while a 438-byte *question* was not.

Nothing caught it earlier. `apiclient.InputRequest.Validate` checks structure
only (every question answered, one value for a single-select), so the TUI answer
form passed its own validation and then failed on the round trip. There is no
`vincent answer` subcommand, so the TUI and raw HTTP are the only two ways in and
both hit the same bound. Mid-run input exists only on the claude adapter
(`SupportsInput` is permanently false for codex and cursor), which is exactly
where questions over 256 bytes are routine.

**The fix** splits the constant. `answers` keys take a new `maxAnswersKeyBytes`,
sized like the answer value they arrive beside rather than like an identifier;
`boundTaskFields`/`boundMap` keep `maxFieldKeyBytes = 256` for `fields`. This is
a change to the broken function, not a guard at the call site.

Nothing becomes unbounded: the route still reads at `maxLargeRequestBytes`
(4 MiB), and `boundAnswers` still applies `maxFieldCount` (100) and
`maxValueCount` (100) per answer. The error message still names the field and the
limit without echoing the key — `boundString` never echoes, and `truncKey` guards
the value-side field name.

Introduced by 2b969f5 (`fix(api): require one JSON document per request and bound
the body`, #140), which added both `maxFieldKeyBytes` and `boundAnswers`; nothing
has touched either since.

## Related

Closes #197

Amends `docs/spec.md` §13.1 in place with a dated note (2026-08-26, issue #197).
The spec was not wrong — its #140 amendment names the bounded fields without
fixing numbers for them — but it did not say the two keys are bounded
*separately*, and after this change that distinction is load-bearing, so it is
recorded there. No decision in `docs/tasks/` or the closed v0 ledger covers the
shared constant.

## How the regression test would catch this coming back

`TestAnswerLongQuestion` (`internal/api/actions_test.go`) is the red test. It
parks a task in `awaiting_input` on a 438-byte question and answers it through
the real `POST /v1/tasks/{id}/answer` handler, asserting 200, the task back in
`running`, and `pending_input` cleared. It was run against the unfixed code and
failed exactly as reported:

```
--- FAIL: TestAnswerLongQuestion (0.35s)
    actions_test.go:616: answer a 438-byte question: 400 {"error":{"code":"validation_failed",
        "message":"answers key must be at most 256 bytes (got 438)"}}, want 200
```

Any future change that puts an identifier-sized bound back on the `answers` key
turns that 200 back into a 400 and the test fails on the same line with the same
message. It builds its question by asserting `len(q) > maxFieldKeyBytes`, so it
cannot quietly stop testing the bound if that constant is retuned.

`TestFieldsKeyBoundUnchanged` is its guard rail, and the reason the fix cannot be
"relax the bound". It passed before this change and still passes: a `fields` key
of 257 bytes on `POST /v1/tasks` is still `400 validation_failed`. Widening
`maxFieldKeyBytes` instead of splitting it would make the red test pass and this
one fail.

`TestEngineLongQuestionRoundTrip` (`internal/taskrun/input_test.go`) is the
end-to-end leg the issue asked for, driven by a new `FAKEAGENT_ASK_LONG=1` knob
on fakeagent's `ask-question` scenario (`askQuestion` previously hard-coded a
short question). The agent asks a 367-byte question, the engine parks the task,
and the test answers it keyed off the text the daemon actually parked on — not
off a literal — which is what a human answering the form does. It then asserts
the result summary echoes both the question and the answer, proving the key
survived the trip out to the CLI and back.

To be straight about what that third test is worth: it passes on the unfixed
code too, because `runner.Answer` does not go through the API's `boundAnswers`.
It is not a second red test. What it pins is the premise the fix rests on — that
the key round-trips verbatim through the agent, the engine and back — so a future
change that starts truncating or normalising the question text anywhere on that
path fails here rather than silently reintroducing an unanswerable question by
another route.

No assertion was weakened anywhere. The two tests in `internal/api` are committed
as they were written and run; the fix commit does not touch them.

## Checklist

- [x] PR title is plain language (no Conventional Commit prefix)
- [x] Commits follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) — `test(api):` for the red test, `fix(api):` for the fix
- [x] Tests added/updated for behavior changes
- [ ] User-visible changes noted under `## [Unreleased]` in `CHANGELOG.md` — **deliberately not done.** `RELEASING.md` (lines 105-114) states that `CHANGELOG.md` carries no `Unreleased` section on purpose: Release Please inserts each new version directly beneath the preamble, so prose parked under `Unreleased` ends up *below* the release it describes. The changelog is written once, on the Release Please PR, and the `fix(api):` commit here is what feeds it. This is a user-visible bug fix and it does belong in the changelog — via that route, not this one.
- [x] Affected page under `docs/` updated — `docs/reference/api.md` splits the "one `fields` / `answers` key" row into two rows with their own limits and says why they differ; `docs/spec.md` §13.1 carries the dated amendment

## Documentation audit

A separate pass checked every derivation `CLAUDE.md` names, and found nothing
further to change — no documentation commit is on this branch, because the two
pages that needed amending were amended in the fix commit itself.

`docs/reference/api.md` is the only page that publishes these bounds (a tree-wide
grep for `256` turns up nothing else but SHA-256 and the TUI's 256 KB transcript
tail), and spec §13.1 is the only record that describes them without fixing
numbers. Everything else was already true and was left alone: no route, CLI
command, config key, TUI binding, `Reason*` constant, step type or adapter
capability changed, so `configuration.md`, `cli.md`, the `tui.md` key tables, the
block-reason tables, `workflow-schema.md`, `task-lifecycle.md` and `agents.md`
are all untouched by design. `troubleshooting.md`'s "A task is stuck in
`awaiting_input`" entry never claimed the daemon might refuse a valid answer, so
it gets no paragraph about a bug it never described.

Three specific negatives worth a reviewer's eye:

- **No gate walkthrough changed.** `scripts/m2-gate.sh` builds its answer body
  from `pending_input` with jq rather than from a literal, and fakeagent's
  default question is still the short one — `FAKEAGENT_ASK_LONG` is off unless a
  test sets it — so the gate exercises exactly what it did before.
- **`skills/vincent-workflows/SKILL.md` is not out of date.** It is runtime text
  spliced into the `create-workflow` prompt, so it would be part of this PR if
  the schema had moved. It did not: no step type, field, validation rule,
  template variable or human-interaction mechanism changed, and the skill tree
  publishes no byte bounds at all.
- **No screenshot is stale.** No TUI code is in the change set, so no captured
  panel can have drifted; `scripts/screenshots.sh` was not run and did not need
  to be.

## Second bug noticed, not fixed here

Not a bug, but worth a reviewer's eye and out of scope for a bug fix:
`apiclient.InputRequest.Validate` validates answer *structure* client-side while
the length rule lives only server-side, which is why the TUI form accepted a
submission the daemon then rejected. That split is fine now that the bound is
sized correctly, but it is the reason this failed at the round trip rather than
in the form, and any future field bound on this path will behave the same way.
